To rescue a high-HP basic pokemon, usually a tank like Snorlax or Chansey, after it has high damage. Your own energy drop should be from a pokemon who needs it the least, and the opponent pokemon selected should be one where this would really cost it, usually the active one. A very standard card that our bot will do fine with. Strikes Back is more of a passive punishment for killing it that's hard to strategize for other than the nuisanse it is just by existing

To be used only when the active pokemon expects to take damage on the next turn, and only damage that's survivable with the Defender attached. Defenders also block self-damage, so they can be used strategically there as well (our game does not block self-damage yet with Defender but it should). The best time to use it is when it would save a valuable active pokemon that would otherwise die. Should not be played just because it exists in the bot's hand.
To be in decks that require energy funnels, or in multi-type decks where a desired energy can be rescued from discard if running short
To be in most decks, and save a pokemon from a missed turn from an opponent's status move. It especially loves decks with pokemon that apply status conditions to themselves, like Vileplume
Not a useful card. Autobuilder should avoid

To be used strategically but not be held onto like it's in a vault. The best times are when your own pokemon would fall 10 damage short of knocking out the opponent, or when an additional 10 damage would result in 1 fewer turn to kill the opponent, as in a move doing 30 damage attacking a pokemon with 70 HP. The best practice there is to plant to hit for 30 on the first turn and use the PlusPower for 40 on the second turn. If you might not survive until the second turn, the PlusPower could probably be used early
Best if the autobuilder avoids

To be used to revive a tank, and not much else. Best if the autobuilder avoids
The same logic as base1 Magnemite and other Kamakaze Timers. Thunder Wave is used as a status lock until that's needed

To heal a moderate amount of damage at the cost of 1 tempo of energy. Should not be used to save a pokemon that it would prevent from powering up enough to attack, as that would just be stalling for no benefit
To be used right away and exist in almost every deck. Weak decks have 1-2, stronger decks have 3-4

To be used liberally and strategically. Do not remove an energy just to remove an energy, do it to something that it would inconvenience by having to re-attach. The opponent's active pokemon usually makes for the best target, but something powerful on the bench could work as well. Denying the active pokemon forces the opponent to re-power that one instead of preparing the bench, might lead to the opponent taking an extra turn to attack, and might completely stop the opponent if he doesn't have any extra energies. After a pokemone is selected, if it has multiple energy types, DCE should be the first target and its own energy type (as in the hard requirements for its moves rather than the colorless extras) should be the second.

To drag in a damaged bench pokemon to finish it off, preferably a strong one that could pose a menace. Bringing in a high damage pokemon from the bench with low HP can still lay a large hit on you before you have a turn to finish it off, and this card allows you to preempt that. It can also shift a dangerous pokemon out of the active spot and replace it with something else that doesn't have the energy to attack or retreat yet.
To not be used to heal only 10 damage unless that has the immediate potential to be life saving (and the pokemon is worth saving)

To retreat a high value pokemon without paying the retreat cost, or launch a sudden switch for a quick attack that the opponent wasn't expecting. Does not want to be used on a free-retreat cost pokemon and prefers heavier retreat costs to nullify. Should not be played just because it exists in the bot's hand

To never use Minimize. Metronome is a Copy Effects move that requires a Setup Turn to actually copy the target move, but the very low energy cost makes it worth it. It could potentially copy a Charizard's attack on the first turn (as long as the Charizard can't attack on its turn to kill it), and then use it against the Charizard on the next turn with only 1 energy and no discards. It just needs to survive long enough to copy and then use on separate turns. Hates coming in against cards with only weak attacks or ones that don't do damage at all

Swords Dance is a Setup Turn move that eats a turn in order to deal double damage with Slash on the next turn. This balances out to the same damage total each way, so best strategy is to only use Swords Dance at exactly 2 energies when a third can be attached for Slash on the next turn. Otherwise, it's better to deal the guaranteed Slash damage each turn

To stall, not attack or retreat. It can't be affected by status conditions, making it a very effective tank. Its attack is decent for what it is, but shouldn't be powered up by the bot when preparing evolutions on the bench is available instead due to its high cost. It exists to eat damage, eat turns, and then die. Likes decks with Alakazam, because that allows it to eat the active pokemon's damage from the bench. Likes playing against Psychic type decks because it's resistant, making it the ultimate tank against those decks (applies to Chansey as well)

Water Gun asks to Over-Attach two extra energies for extra damage, and should be seen as the primary attack. Quick Attack has two use cases: When Water Gun can't be afforded, and when Vaporeon is played in a non-water deck. The latter is viable because Quick Attack only requires Colorless energy, meaning it can be used in any deck if the user is okay never having access to Water Gun. Does well in multi-type decks with other Eevee-lutions.

To use its pokemon power to change its type to whatever the defending pokemon is weak to. This should happen at the first opportunity, as its attack is underwhelming even with its layered status chances without it. It probably shouldn't change its type arbitrarily though; if the opponent has no weakness it should just stay in its current type. But due to this type changing, its attack can be considered 20 dmg instead of 10 in most cases. Maybe the bot can calculate damage ahead of time by assuming Venomoth is already whatever the defender is weak to, as it will be by the time it attacks.

Its attack Damage Scales by the amount of damage the opponent has taken, so it can be a very effective finisher. It's a tank against strong things and flimsy against weak things.
Opponent bench pokemon to deal sneaky damage to. Targets vulnerable ones.

Leer is the primary as it turns Rhyhorn into a very good staller. Horn Attack should only be powered up if it's planning to evolve, but takes over the primary position once powered. 3 energy on Rhyhorn usually translates into an evolution though, so this doesn't happen much.

Peck is primary. 3 energies is a lot to want to attach to a pokemon as weak as Spearow just for a chance at Mirror Move, and Spearow's HP is so low that a copied attack that it previously survived would probably not do much damage. It shouldn't even try to power this up unless readying itself for evolution
Stun Spore is primary, due to its HP being too low to benifit much from Leech Life's healing.
To be used right away

Mega Punch is the primary since having enough Nidokings on the bench for Boyfriends to be effective is unrealistic, even for a human player actively attempting to do it. The bot should only use this if energies don't allow for Mega Punch, and I think the bot will probably get this right already

Hurricane is the most disruptive attack in the game so far and should be preferred in all cases. Pidgeot loves to fight because of its harrassement potential, and it has high value in the active spot and low value on the bench

To usually only power up Irongrip. Guillotine does good damage but is expensive, and its energies are usually better applied elsewhere. If nothing else needs it, then Pinsir becomes happy to have Guillotine powered up, after which it becomes the primary attack

To evolve before most opponent pokemon due to its evolution blocking other evolutions for both players. Prefers a deck with a lot of no-evolve pokemon to maximize the advantage. Hates fighting unless a duplicate exists because keeping its pokemon power active is too valuable to risk losing.

To Over-Attach energy for Water Gun, which is used as the primary attack. As long as it doesn't cost an extra turn in terms of killing the opponent, Lapras will try to confuse with Confuse Ray as well. Performs the function of a tank but fully invests in its attacks, unlike most other tanks, which is why it's not labeled as one. A high value single-stage pokemon for the autobuilder
Kamikaze Timing pattern in the same shape as others with self-destruct. Like those, potential bench self-kills and opponent kills should be factored into the weight.

To only use Dive Bomb since Wildfire asks for an Energy Funnel just to discard the opponent's next card(s) in the deck, and is nowhere near a good tradeoff unless the opponent's deck is close to empty (then it suddenly gains a lot of value). This will be excedingly rare though and might be a waste of time to tune. Its main attack is expensive and is a 50/50 chance of landing, making this card nearly useless. If the autobuilder wants a Moltres, it should take a different variant.

Very valuable against decks with passive pokemon powers, which is common in the Team Rocket set but doesn't get much play elsewhere. Most useful to nullify Aerodactyl, Mr. Mime, or Charizard's ability to attach DCE, which are not in every deck of their energy type. Muk's main attack is decent though, so the autobuilder shouldn't ignore.

To come in against an opponent with 3 or more bench pokemon in order to take full advantage of its attack. As multiple bench pokemon can be damaged, it's best practice to choose already-damaged ones, ones with low HP that you can kill across multiple turns, and stronger ones that you might want to pre-weaken a little.

To use Thunderstorm and weight potential bench damage over potential self-damage, unless close to death itself. Self-kills allow the opponent first strike against your replacement pokemon, so it'll affect your next fighter negatively as well. Depending on potential benefits of the attack, it's sometimes best to pass rather than take a self-kill.

Poison Fang is the primary. Terror Strike's logic follows the same shape as Ninetales' Lure, except with a small amount of damage dealt first. That damage still does not weight it above Poison Fang, but also makes Arbok more willing to enter in situations that force its use than Ninetales is to enter when only Lure is available
Spike Cannon is primary. Already confirmed that the bot handles correctly as it even corrected my original logic here

To always use Lick in every situation, except the extremely rare scenario of not having enough energies in hand for building the bench/evolving Gastly while those energies do exist in the discard pile. We probably don't need to teach the bot Energy Conversion due to the rarity of its use cases. Gastly should still accept the second energy though because it's needed for evolution. If not hoping to evolve, no second energy.

Wing Attack should be primary even if Golbat has damage that can be removed with Leech Life, so 30 offensive damage should outweigh 20 offensive damage + 20 healing. Leech Life becomes preferred if its healing will allow Golbat to survive until its next turn, when it would otherwise die. The damage potential of the next turn should be factored into the decision, as 20 offensive damage + 30 on the next turn is preferable to just doing 30 this turn and dying.

A deck that is a combo Water/Psychic type, but is perfectly viable in just water. Should be avoided in just Psychic. Hyper Beam is an Energy Denial move, and those should always be weighted highly due to turning every turn into an Energy Funnel for the opponent. Works even better if the opponent's move is already an energy funnel. If it is not in a deck with P type energy, its other move isn't usable and doesn't need to be tuned. If both are available it's a standard Attack Choice in the shape of several others, including Dragonair

Kamikaze Timing pattern in the same shape as others with self-destruct. Like those, potential bench self-kills and opponent kills should be factored into the weight. Should never, ever retreat unless retreating prevents an outright loss due to its astronomical retreat cost (and kamikazes should very rarely be retreated anyway).

Harden only if Rock Throw is not available or if a turn is needed to stall. Not indefinite stalling like Kangaskhan or another tank, but intentional stalling like it needs another turn before it can be powered up enough to evolve.

Crabhammer is usually primary but Flail follows the same Damage Scaling pattern as anything with Rage, and can potentially overtake Crabhammer in terms of damage dealt. The bot should be fine as long as it doesn't retreat in this position, which based on observed behavior, it might.

An opening role, as it's one of the best openers available. Smokescreen has the potential to deny an attack, and Smog has a chance to poison. Similar to Beedrill, use Smog when opponent is not poisoned, Smokescreen after it is or before Smog is ready. If opening, it's perfectly valid to give that second energy to the bench instead if something high value is already available or can be evolved realistically quickly.

To evolve on the bench and use its Pokemon Power to Step In at an opportune time. Its attack is relatively underwhelming for what it is but can be powered up quickly in a deck with available DCE. Step In, if used well, can make up for this to some degree too, but is useless if Dragonite evolves in the active spot, which it might considering how useful Dragonair's attacks are.
Water Gun asks for an Over-Attach of up to two additional energies. As long as the bot can do that freely and purposefully, it should handle this card fine
Fury Swipes preferred due to damage potential. Slash should only be used when a guaranteed 20 dmg is needed and rarely ever else

Water Gun asks for an Over-Attach in the same pattern as Omastar. Normal Attack Choice decisions after that, with Agility's potential damage denial being preferred unless Water Gun's added damage can kill or cost fewer turns to get to a kill

To hide on the bench and take damage away from the active pokemon, rather than fight itself. Its attack is decent but it'll often already have stolen damage on it, as its pokemon power is more valuable than its attack. The bot should use it every turn where it's viable, but avoid actually killing Slowbro with it
Pretty useless, autobuilder should avoid. Jellyfish Sting is primary, bot probably does fine.
Another Kamikaze Timer with Selfdestruct, same pattern as the others. Bench damage is guaranteed to both benches rather than a coin flip
To open, as it's an excellent status-locker. Poison first with Spit Poison and then switch to Wrap, in the same pattern as Beedrill
Coin luck for doing any damage at all. Would much rather be on the bench collecting energy to evolve.
Almost no situation where Minimize would be used due to a 50/50 attack denial chance coming from Nasty Goo.

Both Dark Mind and its pokemon power follow Hypno's bench damage logic. Its pokemon power should look to move damage from an injured pokemon on the bench to the active one if it results in a quicker death, or away from the active (or another bench pokemon) and onto a vulnerable bench pokemon. Taking damage away from the opponent's active should account for what the new HP would be after it loses that 10 dmg, and should not be done if that results in an additional turn required to kill it. Killing an opponent's active pokemon with its pokemon power (rather than an attack) is a situation it loves and should possibly even aim for, as that gives it a free attack against the replacement. A bot on the other side of that should be able to recognize it and try to avoid it by healing or retreating, as giving the opponent first attack against a fresh pokemon should be a high weight to avoid, overriding even the unwillingness to spend a retreat cost in many cases. This is why a post-attack poison death (right before the opponent's turn) and a self-kill are rated low as well.
To sneaky knock out opponents using bench damage or its Pokemon Power

To sit on the bench and wait for an evolution, though its pokemon power does help it survive if forced to fight. This should not be counted on though, and it hates a fighting evolution due to low HP and the energy disparity between itself and Kabutops
Call for Family follows the same pattern as with Bellsprout
To Over-Attach two additional energies, though it prefers to stay on the bench and evolve. Its pokemon power is passive but shouldn't factor into decisions.

To play in a combined Water/Psychic deck if Golduck (from this set or Team Rocket) is there too. Does just fine in a water-only deck but can't use Headache if it does, which should should rarely be used anyway
To Confuse with Supersonic first, deny damage with Hide in Shell second.

Space Out is the primary attack due to the Energy Funnel cost of Scavenge. Scavenge should be useful if a specific Trainer card is wanted from the discard pile that could benefit the player more than anything that can be done with Slowpoke at the time, as Slowpoke likely won't survive to evolve after using this.

To escape to the player's hand using its pokemon power when the situation looks bad for it. This can happen mid-turn so the turn-loss of a 'Teleport'-type move shouldn't be a factor. This is free so it should be done rather than letting Tentacool be killed on the next turn, unless there's a need to stall for one additional turn at the cost of sacrificing Tentacool instead
Confusing with Supersonic first is the most valuable move. Once the opponent is confused, Leech Life becomes preferred.

The same function as Scoop Up, except it only applies to the bench and cards are shuffled back into the deck rather than the player's hand. GBC didn't give this to the CPU decks, and I don't think we should either

To exist in multiple numbers in decks with more than one energy type. Used very easily and possibly by default just because it exists in the bot's hand. The best time is when a specific variety of energy is needed at the time but lacked in its owner's hand. Its weight when an energy is not immediately needed could come from the fact that it removes an additional card from the deck, meaning desired cards have one less card to contend with for being drawn by the RNG on subsequent turns. That weight inverts as the number of cards in its user's deck gets lower. If we do this right, the bot should be forced to make difficult decisions in situations where it draws an Energy Search, desperately needs energy, but is running low on cards in its deck. A test of our success might be the bot doing a variety of different choices here based on all the other factors around it, though the situation won't be super common.

To punch above its weight while stalling for an evolution, as it's a very competent fighter that might even be overpowered for an evolving Stage 1. Its pokemon power requires a coin flip for damage to land, so the bot should factor that in to promotion decisions. Playing this guy without an evolution ready is a valid choice, though it should still choose to evolve rather than stay as a Haunter when it doesn have the option. The autobuilder should limit the number of these in deck for balance rather than because it's a bad card, but not avoid them entirely. Maybe combine with other Haunter variants instead of keeping it consistent in either direction.

Trigger conditions should be the same as Professor Oak, but its usefulness should be weighted lower. Hand cards get returned to the deck rather than sent to the discard pile, but this means a tails not only gives you a worse hand but also adds more noise to the deck's remaining RNG pool, though you don't have to worry about burning as many cards as you can before discarding your hand like with Oak.
To be used liberally and resurrect valuable pokemon or a needed evolution card

To sit on the bench and not be put in the active spot unless used to stall, which will normally only provide a single extra turn, but does not give the opponent a prize for killing it. Its preferred spot is the bench, where it's Over-Attached with energy needed for its eventual evolution, if planning to evolve it
To use Stretch Kick whenever High Jump Kick isn't available or when it can kill something on the bench. Otherwise, High Jump Kick is a very high value move.

Rarely ever uses Prophecy, as it doesn't want to enter a match when Dark Mind isn't available. Dark Mind should be used to deal steady bench damage to whatever is vulnerable, even choosing to build up damage on a bench pokemon over multiple turns. Weak things like Magikarp or something already close to death are preferred. The next priority after that is to pre-damage something strong that hasn't entered the fight yet.
Absorb is primary and should be built up to. As long as that happens, it's a classic Attack Choice for the bot that it will probably get correct

To hit and run with Teleport Blast. Attack the opponent and escape to the bench behind sacrificial fodder or a tank (fodder allows a quick return at the cost of giving the opponent a prize). A low/zero retreat cost pokemon that can eat the attack is also an option. Mind Shock is useful when the opponent is resistant to Psychic type or if the added 10 damage can result in a kill. If the opponent is not a threat, Dark Alakazam can hang in there and Mind Shock

To jump in mid-game and surprise a strong, evolved, and powered-up opponent pokemon with Fling, sending all the cards back into the opponent's deck. It does not want to use Mega Punch and does not want to be put in a position where it will ever be forced to use Mega Punch unless the opponent is on their last pokemon

To use Magnetic Lines to sweep energy away from the opponent's active pokemon each turn and onto the most useless looking bench pokemon. Not one like Magikarp that can evolve strong and be aided in its evolution by additional energies. Preferably a non-evolving one like Electabuzz who doesn't benefit much from additional energies, pushing as many as it can onto these targets. If the opponent pokemon is already as powered up as they will need to be, additional energy attachments become free. It only needs Sonicboom when the opponent is resistant to Electric type

To time its evolution in order to resurrect high value pokemon from the discard pile. Its attack is very under powered and using it is almost a throwaway of the card while trying to inflict a 50/50 shot at a medium amount of damage, which can be more valid than retreating.

To strategically deny the opponent's use of trainer cards by simply existing, meaning its evolution involves timing since it blocks your own trainers too. Its attack has high damage potential but almost guarantees death on the next turn. Therefore its best place is on the bench, holding off trainer usage. It should only be sent in when its trainer-blocking abilities are no longer wanted, no longer needed, if a duplicate exists on the bench, if your need to try for large damage quickly becomes great enough. It prefers a deck that intentionally does not use many trainer cards in order to use this denial as a strategy.

To ruin a strong opponent pokemon's day by showing up and using Stun Gas, where Poisoning is the opponent's best possible outcome. It likes to live in a deck full of Koffings and Weezings/Dark Weezings, and if enough exist on the bench at the same time, it can become a competent attacker with Mass Explosion, with a maximum of 80 dmg if all four Koffings/evolutions are in play, which is enough to one-shot almost any other "dark" pokemon
To check the opponent's hand and get rid of the most dangerous Trainer card there

A low/zero retreat cost pokemon that can eat the attack is also an option. Mind Shock is useful when the opponent is resistant to Psychic type or if the added 10 damage can result in a kill. If the opponent is not a threat, Dark Alakazam can hang in there and Mind Shock

To deal bench damage and poison the opponent at the same time with Poison Vapor. Stare is used before Dark Arbok is powered up enough for Poison Vapor or if there is an actively disruptive Pokemon Power on the opponent's bench, like Aerodactyl's Prehistoric Power. This is a much more menacing card than the 10 damage number on its face suggests, though its HP is low

To deal bench damage and poison the opponent at the same time with Poison Vapor. Stare is used before Dark Arbok is powered up enough for Poison Vapor or if there is an actively disruptive Pokemon Power on the opponent's bench, like Aerodactyl's Prehistoric Power. This is a much more menacing card than the 10 damage number on its face suggests, though its HP is low
Hydrocannon wants Over-attach. Attack Choice between that and Rocket Tackle once powered up enough
Wants Coin Luck for Continuous Fireball, and to Over-Attach as many energies as possible (though maybe not more than 8 or so) for additional chances at Coin Luck
Loves to come from the bench to summon additional pokemon when the bench is low. Other than that it depends on luck, as it's low HP and its attack is all or nothing
A Bench Engine that wants to hang out on the bench in high numbers, multiplying the number of 20 Dmg coin flips a retreating opponent pokemon must go through

Attacks vulnerable bench pokemon through its pokemon power and Flitter. Flitter can also hit the opponent's active pokemon if beneficial. Low HP so best use-cases might be quick cheap kills. It's hard to keep a vulnerable pokemon safe from this one, but it's hard to keep Dark Golbat safe after it strikes.

Uses Ice Beam to try to hold the opponent in place. Its Pokemon Power means that a fully powered-up Dark Gyarados has a 50/50 chance upon death to deal 60 dmg to its attacker. It also has the potential to Over-Attach energies to deal even more potential damage upon death, with the aim of being just enough to take its attacker with it. However, the 50/50 chance should make this a secondary investment, with the primary investment still being readying the bench

To come in after the opponent has a full or mostly full bench and deal high potential damage with Bench Manipulation, preferably as a surprise against a strong opponent pokemon. It does not want to use Psypunch, unless no pokemon exist on the bench or it evolved from Drowzee while in the active spot and does not have the required energy for its main attack yet.

It does not want to use Mega Punch and does not want to be put in a position where it will ever be forced to use Mega Punch unless the opponent is on their last pokemon

To evolve rather than attack, but is capable of having a 50/50 chance at dealing a high amount of surprise damage. It is extremely vulnerable after attacking so it should avoid having to. If it's ever in a position where it has to use Tail Slap, it's either extremely safe, the opponent has 20 HP or less remaining (as it's guaranteed damage for a finisher rather than a coin flip), or if something went very very wrong. Fireball specifies that it can ONLY be used if there's at least one R energy attached, but the attack costs RRR. Therefore, I think this implies that it excludes Rainbow in terms of requiring at least one actual R energy to be used, and that the real R energy would have to be the one discarded on a successful attack.

To evolve whenever it wants by using its Pokemon Power to summon a Dark Dragonite from the deck, or even aid other bench pokemon by summoning their evolutions. It can even be thrown into the active spot, summon its own evolution, and evolve in the same turn, so it's smart to pre-load enough energy for what Dark Dragonite might need. It should very rarely stay unevolved in the active spot long enough to use its own attack. This would mean it's in action before it's ready.

To stall for a small amount of time against a weaker opponent or deal some quick damage before loading up the bench. Energy Bomb's usage will transfer both/all of its energies to bench pokemon however its user would like, but means Dark Electrode will have to wait two turns to use it again, during which time it'll likely be killed. Rolling Tackle should only be used if it isn't ready to use Energy Bomb or it's not an opportune time with survival until the opportune time seeming likely.

Uses Playing with Fire as the main attack, which requires a single R energy discard each use, which requires the player to invest their only energy attachment each turn to keep it going. Once it takes enough damage, Rage can become a viable alternative. Card wording contains the same R energy caveat as Dark Charmeleon

Pollen Stench is a gamble in terms of Confusing the opponent vs itself. Therefore it wants to be used after the opponent has already been poisoned by Poisonpowder, or if it seems like Poison Powder will not be able to be used.

Super Psy is a high damage attack and it wants to be used. Third Eye is much cheaper but requires an energy discard, meaning it should only be used when the player doesn't want to power up to Super Psy. If it was about to be killed on the opponent's next turn and cannot afford Super Psy, that would be a good time.

Is not afraid to enter right after evolving or unpowered, or even from a quick evolution from an Eevee opener. Lighting Flash is an excellent stalling attack while it builds up energy for Thunder Attack, which should become the primary attack after. Thunder Attack has a 50/50 chance at 10 self-damage, so Lightning Flash becomes cheaper again if it can get a clean kill or 10 self-damage might kill Dark Jolteon and Kamazake is decided against.

Its Pokemon Power wants to be used liberally, but only if there are duplicate cards in the hand that can be cheaply dumped. Dumping energy cards from the hand can be cheap or expensive depending on how many others are currently required for bench evolutions and exist in the hand.
Wants Coin Luck for Continuous Fireball, and to Over-Attach as many energies as possible (though maybe not more than 8 or so) for additional chances at Coin Luck

To leave a copy strategically unevolved on the bench, as long as the evolved version is also available. If one is available on the bench and powered up, it has the potential to jump in at any time and auto-kill any pokemon on the opponent's bench with 20 HP or less remaining by draggin them into the active spot. It can also do the reverse where it damages the active opponent and throws that pokemon back to the bench, so these should be chosen based on the situaiton. Due to their energy cost, powering up before an evolution exists in the hand is viable in case it needs to enter and land a cheap shot

Prevents the opponent from leaving when it's in the active spot. There aren't many situaitons where this is beneficial but it can be sometimes. If it's obvious the opponent will want to retreat rather than let a pokemon be killed, it's a good idea to move Dark Muk to the active spot to stop it if it's something high value. It should be prioritized as a poisoner over that.

To be a better card because it's pretty useless for a Stage 1, and the autobuilder should probably avoid it. Only uses Fascinate when there is not enough energy for Poison Claws and the options on the bench would be the same or preferable.

Coin Luck and a Setup Turn, so it can deal decent damage, confuse itself, and then flip heads to deal high damage on the next turn. If it flips tails, it (likely) kills itself and gives the opponent first attack against the replacement pokemon. And that's if its 60 HP even survives the setup turn.

To use Flame Pillar only if it finds doing 10 dmg to the bench worth having to use your only energy attachment to recharge its R energy on your next turn. Right before it's about to die is a good time, as well as right before an opp. bench pokemon is about to die. There is almost no situation where Rear Kick should be used.
To use Whirlpool as a primary attack to force the opponent to discard energies, which is a very effective form of harrassment. Bite should be used when it can kill but Whirlpool can't.
To use Mirror Shell any turn it thinks it's about to die. Doesn't like to fight unless used as a trap

To power up for evolution before the evolution card is in hand. It wants to evolve on the bench but if an evolution card never shows up, it can switch to the active spot and summon its own evolution card from the deck using Rapid Evolution. This costs its attack for the turn though, so the cost is a free hit from the opponent on the evolved pokemon.

To assist the next turn by changing the opponent pokemon's type to be weak to your deck or the next pokemon you want to bring in. Porygon will likely die on the next turn so it comes at the price of a prize. If Porygon isn't killed, it has a free retreat cost, and should do so immediately to switch with the planned attacker, before becoming available to be used again. Things are going either very poorly or very well if Psybeam gets charged up, let alone used. Autobuilder should avoid
Psyshock to be its primary attack. Vanish is almost never used unless about to die and prizes are short
Loves to come from the bench to summon additional pokemon when the bench is low. Other than that it depends on luck, as it's low HP and its attack is all or nothing

To use its Pokemon Power to attach an extra energy needed before evolving. It can open a game, attach an energy Turn 1 and use Fire Tail, and then its next turn attach a second energy, use Gather Fire to attach a third, and then evolve and use Charmeleon's three-energy attacks right away
To use Hyper Fang even though it's 50/50 to land, Gnaw is weaker than Hyper Fang landing half the time. Gnaw becomes useful when a guaranteed 20 damage is needed for a kill

To open a game by wreaking havok on the bench while it itself hopes to evolve. Both attacks are good ones for a basic vs basic matchup, and Scratch is also worth investing in. Even when Scratch is powered up, Dig Under should be considered when a bench strike can earn a kill in the next couple turns.
To not start a match unless theres a DCE ready to attach. Would prefer to evolve on the bench

Its Pokemon Power is a gamble so it doesn't want to be used as a default. If the player won't be able to attack this turn anyway, that might be a very good time to take the chance. Worth keeping on the bench for that reason. Nightmare along with its 50 HP doesn't make it a bad opener either, but sitting on the bench is where it's most valuable. The card text does not state a limit, so a valid strategy would be to have multiple of these on the bench for multiple chances and putting an opponent to sleep on a turn where you already couldn't attack
Only wants to open if an evolution and realistic energy path is in hand. If fighting, which it would prefer to avoid, Tackle is only used if Sand-attack is unaffordable.
Poison Sting is the primary attack but it Poisons on a coin flip. This card would prefer to evolve on the bench but would stand a chance if dragged out against another basic

To open a match as often as it can. Any chance it gets to use Sticky Hands is a good one, even in a sacrific/stalling situation, and Poison Gas is an excellent move to build up to it (though isn't used anymore after Sticky Hands is available)
To fight only if it can survive to evolve. Would prefer the bench. Poison Gas is the primary attack and Tackle is never needed after Poison Gas is affordable

Only wants to open if a DCE is in hand. Otherwise its attacks take to long to build it and it's better off sitting on the bench to evolve. If you already have a deck that uses DCE and the Machamp line, this card will be an asset above all other Machop cards. Otherwise it's worse than the base1 Machop.
A Bench Engine that wants to hang out on the bench in high numbers, multiplying the number of 20 Dmg coin flips a retreating opponent pokemon must go through

To open only if a DCE is already in-deck and in-hand. Otherwise the bench is where it belongs. There are very few occasions where Magnetism would be useful and I suspect our bot would get it right without extra planning

Doesn't want to fight. Might not survive long enough to use Anger if opening, might not survive to its next turn if brought in to use Anger later. Would prefer the bench. Mischief is only used if Anger can't be.
Prefers not to open without a DCE in hand

Loves to open. Uses Sleep Powder when it wants to cost the opponent a turn, and uses Poisonpowder when it wants to do damage. Since Sleep Powder is 50/50 and both attacks have the same energy cost, it's probably better to Poison first and then attempt to put the poisoned pokemon to sleep.

Hates to fight because its attack requires an Energy Funnel, and energy feeding a basic pokemon that you'd rather power up to evolve is a very bad thing. Only worth doing if no other option is available.

To play in a Water/Psychic combo deck, though it would do just fine in Water only (but not Psychic only). Doesn't mind opening, especially in a deck with Psychic energy. Water Gun is an Over-Attach move, though it might be best to not stack energy beyond what Golduck/Dark Golduck will need, unless doing so scores a kill.

Likes to open if its evolution is in hand. There's no way to know if its Pokemon Power is benefiting its user or hurting it, so it can be used liberally by the AI as long as it's not just swapping out the same card over and over.

Loves to open if its evolution is in hand. Headbutt should be used if not planning to evolve, Afternoon Nap should be used if evolution is in hand and survivability until then is realistic, as it's a Setup Turn to steal an extra energy
Probably shouldn't open but isn't the worst option. Wants the bench
Decent evo opener. Prefers the bench if not planning to evolve

Attacks vulnerable bench pokemon through its pokemon power and Flitter. Flitter can also hit the opponent's active pokemon if beneficial. Low HP so best use-cases might be quick cheap kills. It's hard to keep a vulnerable pokemon safe from this one, but it's hard to keep Dark Golbat safe after it strikes.
Might not survive to use Bite if coming in cold. Prefers the bench if evolution isn't realistic
The bot can play this liberally. The only benefit is revealing prizes for both players, which the bot can then use to be strategic in what it takes.
To check the opponent's hand and get rid of the most dangerous Trainer card there
To be used right away to find a desired evolution card. The autobuilder should only put this in decks with multiple cards with "Dark" in its name.
Probably doesn't need additional logic if the bot treats it like Bill. The exception might be holding off if the bench is already full and it doesn't feel like it's desperate for any cards.
To be used when doing 10 dmg to the opponent would mean more than 10 points of self-damage. To be avoided when the bot's own bench has pokemon with only 10 HP remaining
To be played any time the bot has a hand card it doesn't mind throwing away (duplicate, energy card when energy is in abundance, etc)

Should prefer a balance beetween basic, evo, and energy cards as the default. Card families should be prefered when available, like a Staryu -> Starmie, energy should be preferred if a lot of energy has been burned through and the AI is running short
Should be played when its opponent has a passive Pokemon Power currently in use that directly hampers what the AI would like to do. Aerodactyl and Mr. Mime are prime targets
Should not be played against a pokemon that's going to die in the same turn or is already asleep. Other than that, it's a very good thing to play whenever it's received

Uses Ice Beam to try to hold the opponent in place. Its Pokemon Power means that a fully powered-up Dark Gyarados has a 50/50 chance upon death to deal 60 dmg to its attacker. It also has the potential to Over-Attach energies to deal even more potential damage upon death, with the aim of being just enough to take its attacker with it. However, the 50/50 chance should make this a secondary investment, with the primary investment still being readying the bench. If expected to die in the next turn, an additional Over-Attach might actually be desired as long as it's not denying that energy from something on the bench that needs it more.
Coin Luck in terms of dealing high bench damage before it's killed itself. Would prefer several turns to attack the bench without being killed itself, so it likes facing weaker pokemon or tanks.

To come in after the opponent has a full or mostly full bench and deal high potential damage with Bench Manipulation, preferably as a surprise against a strong opponent pokemon. It does not want to use Psypunch, unless no pokemon exist on the bench or it evolved from Drowzee while in the active spot and does not have the required energy for its main attack yet.
To use Thundershock as its main attack and rarely ever use Growl. Similar pattern to other basics

To open and use Cat Punch, which has a 50/50 chance to force the opponent to choose which pokemon to damage on the bench. Our bot should probably weight that slightly below getting to pick its own pokemon to damage
To be ready to evolve even when no evolution cards exist in the hand. Its pokemon power allows it to summon its own evolution whenever an allied pokemon evolves, so timing that can be important.

To disrupt with Energy Control before it's ready to use Telekinesis to hurt the bench. Telekinesis can also hit the active pokemon if desired, so all in play should be considered potential targets that the bot weighs. Energy Control should only be used when Telekinesis can't, and should not be intentionally used as a stalling move. If it is used and successful, energy choices should follow the pattern of Dark Magneton's Electric Lines.

To sit on the bench against status-pressure opponents and heal every status infliction right after it's inflicted. It doesn't like to fight itself, as its attack is weak for its stage and requires a lot of energy, and losing it loses your free status healing (and it can't heal its own status conditions either). Shouldn't even be powered up if other options exist. Prime target for an opponent's Gust of Wind.
Identical to basep-3
To use Texture Magic to become resistant to its opponent, and then use 3-D Attack. If the opponent switches out and is replaced by a new type, first priority becomes changing its resistance again.
To be used only when desperate, as the card drawing also benefits your opponent AND it makes you miss a turn
To only use Poison Claws. Tempt is only useful in the same pattern as Ninetales' Lure, except it relies on a coin flip and should be treated with even less value because of that
To enter play when a lot of pokemon occupy both benches against a strong opponent and attempt a Kamikaze as its main strategy.

To match the opponent's energy amount and use Synchronize, and to otherwise use Pound. The bot should be willing to even Over-Attach a third energy if the opponent pokemon has three energies and could be killed by a 40 dmg move (but not a 10 dmg one)
Quick Attack is primary, Light Screen only if it can't be afforded or won't land damage (like if the opponent protects itself first)
Identical to base3-53
To deal quick damage and be sacrificed, as it's a liability as a sustained attacker.
Straightforward for the bot
Straightforward with bench damage mechanics, nothing fancy
To deal bonus damage every July 31. Probably shouldn't be played any other day as it can't evolve
The bot should try to use Fly most often but will probably be fine on its own
See basep-54 for Thunderbolt logic
Attack Choice, should prefer Agility due to higher damage. Both moves have a 50/50 chance at damage denial
To play in a Water type deck instead of Lightning type

To come in mid-game with energy in the discard pile without even being powered up. As long as two energy exist in discard, it can attach a single energy and use a Setup Turn (Energy Absorbtion attack) to power up the rest of the way, essentially skipping a turn of powerup at the cost of giving the opponent a free attack during the Setup Turn. Having it enter fully powered is a good strategy too. Does not want to fight if there is insufficient energy in the discard pile and doesn't have enough energy for Psyburn on its own.

Thunderbolt deals high damage but costs 3 energy and demands that all be discarded each time. However, Recharge adds an extra energy from the deck, making it a Setup Turn move that recharges Thunderbolt in 2 turns rather than the natural 3. The bot might do fine with this

To sit on the bench and use its Pokemon Power when needed, as its attack makes it a low-value card. The pokemon power should be used every turn, as it allows for the card just drawn from the deck to be the one returned if it's not desirable. The bot should do this each turn and then select from what's in its hand with the drawn card added when choosing what to send back to the deck, prioritizing both strength and current need.

Flames of Rage is a Damage Scaling move that should be treated like a Kamikaze Timer. It requires a double Energy Funnel to maintain, so it should not plan to be maintained. Quick Attack is preferred unless near death, then Flames of Rage becomes valuable. This card should be expected to be lost on the following turn.

To evolve before fighting. If fighting, it only wants to use Double-Edge if there aren't better targets on the bench for those energy cards. If it's already powered up, Double-Edge is the primary attack unles resulting in self-kill

To use Devolution Beam only when the HP reduction from the de-evolved opponent would result in its death. Otherwise, the opponent can just re-evolve it again. Otherwise, Psywave scales in damage based on opponent energy count, and can be a hard hitting attack in certain situations. The bot should calculate that when deciding who to promote.
Identical to basep-8
Nothing special. Classic Attack Choice that our bot can resolve. Clutch prevents retreat but I don't think that needs to be priced.
Full Speed Charge is primary but risks variable recoil damage. Reluctance to use it should probably scale with how many negative coin flips it would need to self-kill

To attempt to use Fairy Power to return a damaged bench card to its player's hand, being willing to sacrifice itself across multiple turns to do so if the Coin Luck doesn't cooperate right away. The bot probalby should not decimate its own bench by doing this every turn though, and only select pokemon with damage. Operates under similar rules as Scoop Up. Moon Impact is an afterthought, or when it needs to be offensive.
Its only attack always deals damage equal to half of the opponent's remaining HP (rounded up). This live counter should be priced into all calclations
To be a tank that also powers up its main attack when viable and realistic to reach. Its effectiveness as a tank goes up when able to attack
One-Two Punch is primary. Child's Punch sucks too much to be a stalling move
To use Moonwatching when its owner's hand is low on energy, even if it has to enter and be sacrificed just for that. Otherwise, Comet Slap becomes primary

To tuse Take Away as a pseudo-Kamikaze Timer, only better because it doesn't involve killing the card. An extremely good eject button to be used when death seems imminent. Blizzard should be used in all other situations.
Standard Attack Choice. Works better if our bot prices DCE in hand as a two energy bump.
Its pokemon power should be priced into damage projection calculations against opponent basic pokemon
Focus Energy is a Setup Turn for Gnaw, but only the first time before Gnaw can be afforded
Nothing special. Mark this as green
Whirlwind follows same logic as other moves of the same name. Razor Wind will probably get priced higher by the bot and I don't want to fight that

To be considered ready for fighting 2 energies away from max rather than the normal 1, but only if another energy already exists on the bench. Its pokemon power allows it to move a single energy from the bench to itself once active, so two energies can be attached to it this turn in total

To possibly use multiple setup turns if there are enough discard pile energies to grab and if it can realistically survive long enough. Not many situations where that would happen though, so we might not need to build it. Best strategy might just be one Charge one Discharge anyway.

An Energy Funnel, but one that supplies the bench and should not be seen as a negative as long as the bench wants energy. Supplying Electric Current on a turn that it can be used should probably even be seen as an equivalent to directly attaching that energy to the intended bench target, if we want to match Pocket's bot. Charge only becomes a Setup Turn move when energy for Electric Current can't be supplied from the hand, and the bot should hate being in that situation.

Confusion Pulse is primary but Removal Pulse is so close in value that we could possibly even deprioritize its powerup very slightly without gating it, if possible. Consider that an extra mile kind of thing
Tackle preferred over Thundershock whenever possible
Charge is a Setup-Turn move for attaching energy, if conditions are met. It would not save a turn but allow an energy to be allocated to the bench that would otherwise have been spent on this card
Same archetype as other Kamikaze Timer electric types. Mega Punch is primary and Thunderbolt is used right before death.
Bot will prob be fine

Faces a unique Attack Choice in that both attacks are valuable. GBC would take the easy way out and weight Fissure over Rock Slide. Hard mode would be to price how quickly Rock Slide could kill bench pokemon against how quickly Fissure could kill the active one.

To sit on the bench as a Bench Engine and absorb a small amount of damage every turn for the active pokemon (passive due to its pokemon power). Prefers not to fight because its main attack needs Coin Luck not to do zero damage

To be used in almost any sitution at almost any energy level. Crosscounter is extremely dangerous, and puts a fresh and highly energized Charizard just a coin flip away from Kamikaze death. Magnum Punch is worth powering up as well, becoming the primary attack once ready. This card is not afraid of coming in fresh and leaning on Crosscounter until powered up though.
Bot should be fine as-is. Standard Attack Choice and Bench Target mechancis
Follows similar logic to many Jungle/Fossil poisoners. Needles should be used to poison. Once poisoned, Sandstorm becomes primary.
Bot will probably be fine. Only light checks probably needed just to be safe
Lucky Shot is primary due to 15 avg dmg vs Tackle's 10. Standard Bench Target mechanics. Bot should be fine
Hook Shot is primary and bypasses resistance. This bypass should be priced in to calculations for the bot
Nothing special. File as clear
Taunt follows Lure logic. Light Kick is primary

Karate Chop is primary but Fidget is okay to be used any turn that Karate Chop can't be, though should never be priced as an attack itself. It's harmless and costs nothing but doesn't provide anything either
All mechanics exist, bot should be fine. Horn Toss is Whirlwind by a different name

Drill Tackle is a 75% success chance rather than a 50/50, and should be priced as such. This card is an OP opener and should be used as a high damage starting card, or in many situations. It's cheap high damage with an only 25% chance of failure
Same logic as base1 Wartortle's Attack Choice
Blocks retreat but that doesn't need pricing imo

To be a Bench Engine that wreaks havok by using its pokemon power every single turn to try to drag a vulnerable bench pokemon out. The exception to this is if the opponent's current active pokemon is a guaranteed kill and there are no higher value kills on the bench. If we don't track kill value based on the treat it removes, we should
To fight, because any attack that damages it results in a 50% chance the opponent will become confused. Its only attack does not involve special strategy
Sprial Dive should price against Dive every turn in terms of damage dealt. Tie goes to Dive unless Spiral Dive can kill a bench pokemon
To only use Psychic Exchange if there are less than 5 cards in its hand and none of them are of particular value, like an impending evolution card
Usage is similar to Rocket's Hitmonchan, minus the Kamikaze aspect.

To come in when multiple bench pokemon have damage on them and use Healing Pollen. Its value is limited by needing to be in a multi-type deck to be worth its space in the deck, as each attack needs a different energy type. If both are available, the damage-dealing one should be used unless healing value outweighs it
To open a game and use Alert right away. Otherwise, Wing Attack should be preferred because Alert would bring in a fresh pokemon to face an attack before it can attack itself
Bot will be fine. Probably green
Vine Whip should be priced above Poison Vine
Takes guaranteed recoil damage, should be priced as such
Deflector onlly if Egg Bomb can't be used or might result in a subpar Kamikaze result
An Over-Attach that isn't supported by its evolution and so shouldn't be priced past the second energy

Magic Pollen in primary and the condition chosen should be Poison if the opponent will be 10 HP away from death after the attack lands. Otherwise, confusion is preferred as it risks damage negation, self-damage, and hindering retreat all in one. If the opponent is already under confusion, Healing Pollen can be used when this card approaches death. If the opponent is not status'd when this card is close to death, attempting to get it status'd takes priority over survival.

Vile Smell is a Setup Turn for *evolution*, since this card will just evolve out of its confusion. Otherwise, Dream Dance is preferred due to the disproportionate chance the opponent will be cost an attack over its user
Its pokemon power is identical to Charizard's but with Grass type. However, this advantage doesn't carry over to its evolutions so it shouldn't be priced
To price in the healing potential of both moves
Stretch Vine is primary, Bench Targeter
To use Flytrap to drag out vulnerable Bench Targets into the active spot to be killed
Vine Whip preferred, Sleep Poison used before Vine Whip is ready

Removal Beam would be primary even without Energy Denial, which it also is. However, it asks for a Psychic energy. If this card's deck does not have that, the C cost for Removal Beam should not be paid either

Attack Choice follows the same pattern as Rocket's Scyther. Pain Amplifier is chosen in almost all situations in which it would result in a bench death. The bot might get this right but worth testing once
To alternate between Screaming Headbutt and Naptime, but only the latter if it has damage on it. Since Screaming Headbutt can't be used two turns in a row, this might naturally work out.
Good Morning primary. Nothing special
Sleight of Hand should be used if low on energy and the number chosen scaling based on need
Its attack is pointless unless it's about to die on the next turn, then its useful for saving the energy. In any other case it would rather pass without attacking
Headbutt primary
Retreat hindrance doesn't need pricing
To get a bias towards entering play when its evolution   line fills the bench. That would mean pricing in the future damage based on what exists on the bench
Shouldn't be deterred too much by the self-sleep

Rebirth should be built as an option and the bot should always accept. It's low HP makes it a spawn camp risk if the bot keeps repeating it against a strong opponent, but this might be too niche to worry about

An uncomfortable amount of energy just for an attack that relies on Coin Luck to avoid yeeting itself straight back into the deck, where all 5 of those energies will need to be attached all over again just for another 50/50 chance. There is no other option. This card sucks
Lava Burst is primary but should be used sparingly as it discards 5 cards from its own deck. This should be priced against remaining card count as the deck lowers

Kindle is an Energy Funnel but it Energy Denies the opponent at the same time. Pricing-wise, I'd say that's a net negative because then this card itself can never power up. It should want to be able to power up to Slash without burning through energy doing Kindle over and over. The best way to avoid this decision at all is to keep it out of the active spot without being ready for Slash
Standard Attack Choice with Lure mechanics on the secondary. Fire Tackle is primary
Has conditional Bench Target conditions that should be priced into damage assessments for bringing it into battle
Agility should be priced to include its chance to prevent damage each turn
Its pokemon power should be used every turn that it has damage on it
Flame should be primary for its guaranteed damage. Quick Attack shouldn't even be built up to on its own unless prepping for evolution
A deck without a large variety of basic pokemon (duplicates rather than different ones). Usage follows normal Stadium logic

To be used when a pokemon is about to die, has energies attached, and the value of the energy saved outweighs any attack that pokemon can make instead, which would be the minority of cases. One that might be valid is something Over-Attached for evolution that will die before it can evolve, removing the excess energy and leaving it with only what it needs to attack. Another use case is when the bot does not have the energy in hand to power up its active pokemon to the desired level or prep it for impending evolution (card in hand), to remove energy from a bench pokemon to then give it to the active one
To be used after a valuable pokemon has been knocked out to put it back in the deck
Same drawing/discarding logic as Secret Mission, though the gamble aspect should be priced as well
A UI setup where the player picks rock, paper, or scissors and the bot comes back with a random selection. If a tie, do it again. Usage logic similar to Professor Oak

Follows logic similar to Professor Oak but cards are re-shuffled into the deck rather than being discarded and should be priced accordingly. Should be played for its benefit to the bot over its disruptive effect on the opponent
Should follow normal Stadium play logic, once we create that
To be played when the bot's current active pokemon doesn't want to retreat itself. Otherwise we don't need to price too much into this
To be used liberally, but only when the opponent has 3 or more cards in their hand. Some situations override, like dumping cards ahead of a Professor Oak usage

To be used in a similar fashion to Switch, in that it should be seen as an escape item primarily. The replacement pokemon should be seen as fodder regardless of what it is, as it's likely to take damage and die before being powered up or evolved. Anything can be used except something highly valuable, but preferred would be something with a 1 energy attack cost that has a status chance
Same as holo variant

Prefers to be used when multiple pokemon have damage on them, but this isn't exclusive. Desperation or an ability to prevent death on the next turn should lower the barrier for use on a single pokemon considerably.
Same as holo variant
The card's conditions are enough to shape the bot's behavoir. Mark as green

I almost don't even want to include this card because we'll have to invent game-wide mechanics for pokemon length tracking just for this one card that isn't even that good. If we figure out how to do it cheaply, the bot should treat the play logic like Bill's. I'm open to many options here including changing the card itself or even just scrapping it

Similar usage to Bill. The bot should be careful with the number of cards it draws when the deck is running out and it has fewer remaining cards than the player. Otherwise, it should always choose to draw three
Same as holo variant

To be used when conditions apply. If forced to discard valuable hand cards to use, that should be priced against the decision though should not outright preclude it. The best time to use this is when it will surprise the opponent by knocking out their pokemon on a turn where it otherwise wouldn't have, destroying their turn-based calculations.
Same as holo variant

Play logic follows normal Stadium rules, though it doesn't want to be in any deck without some of Erika's cards in it because then it would be useless. Stadiums benefit both sides equally but this one disproportionately affects the one who plays it, because the opponent would need Erika cards as well to benefit.
Normal stadium logic. Wants a deck with many pokemon with a 1-energy retreat cost, because this will make a music chairs retreating game free in such a case.
Normal stadium logic
To be in decks with Lt. Surge cards. Damage boost when applicable should be priced into the bot's decisions at all levels

To be used liberally. The card selected should be an evolution card for something it currently has in play, and if not then something it has in its hand. If neither is applicable, it can just pick something. Wants to be in a deck with Brock cards because it's useless otherwise
Similar logic to Brock's Training Method. The card traded should be less valuable ones or duplicates to ones already in play
To be used when there are no basic pokemon in its player's hand. Since the card rules themselves exclude usage at any other time, we don't need to train the bot. Can probably be marked green

To only be used when the bot wasn't going to attack this turn anyway. Otherwise, other conditions aren't really needed. If used against the bot, the card rules handle the logic. WotC ruling - It disables the opponent's entire hand for a turn
Best use case is to put weak pokemon onto your opponent's bench when your own active pokemon deals bench damage. Much too limited to be worth training the bot on

To be played liberally if the opponent has benched pokemon with weight scaling depending on benched pokemon value. The bot should probably resist using it against just an unpowered basic pokemon on the bench but love to use it against something with energy attached, especially something strong or evolved (if evolved, that should add to the weight more than energy)

To be used only when the opponent has fewer prizes than the bot, so that the opponent accepting the treaty doesn't disadvantage the bot. If prizes are equal, it should be weighted low by default but scaled up slightly if the bot's own active pokemon has the advantage over its opponent's active pokemon. If the player uses one, the bot's choice whether or not to accept should be based on the same logic but from the opposite perspective; only accept if it's currently in the lead prize-wise. Not even a tie scenario when on the receiving end.

To have the card selection decision based on which cards it doesn't want to throw away rather than the ones it wants to keep. It should take whatever is most valuable to it at the time, with needed evolutions or energy during a drought getting a boost when applicable

Allows a look at the opponent's hand but I don't think the bot will need to do anything with that info. For discarding and drawing, the bot should first find what it deems duplicate or not valuable and discard them. The number drawn is automatic based on that decision. It should only be careful when running low on cards, following Bill logic there.

Likes to be played when an evolved pokemon can't currently attack but when its prior evolution could with the same energy amount. This applies to cards that have physically been played only, so a pokemon that skips stage 1 by evolving with Pokemon Breeder can't use its stage 1 evolution's moves. Likes decks with cards that require a down turn in between its main attacks, such as Charizard (if not Over-Attached in advance). This would allow Charizard to use Charmeleon's Slash (not Flamethrower since it's an Energy Funnel and defeats the purpose) in the down turn when Charizard would only have 3 energies

A deck with Sabrina cards that involve coin flipping, as that is its only use case. Card rules dictate its usage situations, so risk for the bot is only playing it when a card doesn't want a coin flip this turn. The bot should ask for a re-flip when the result is below the 50/50 odds chance, so if 3 coins are flipped, 1 heads is a re-flip but 2 heads are not. An equal 1/2 or 2/4 situation should not be a re-flip
To play in an all water or mostly water type deck, because its attack damages every non-water pokemon on either bench. Loves to fight because of that. One attack, logic is easy
Coin Luck to land a big hit with Knockout Needle, which is the primary attack. Bot's probably fine

To be a guerrilla fighter. It jumps into active to attempt to poison the opponent with its only attack, before its pokemon power bounces it back to the bench. The 'bail' option should be accepted in most scenarios excpet ones where it can deal disproportionate damage at little risk to itself, or if there are no other viable options on the bench (or more valuable ones).
Tankier than it looks due to its pokemon power. Attack logic is standard, needs some degree of Coin Luck
Water Gun Over-Attaches twice, but should never be used after the first Over-Attach because Bubblebeam becomes affordable is and is primary after that. Same damage plus chance to paralyze
Standard Attack Choice and Bench Target. Probably green
Coin Luck, otherwise its attack does nothing. Probably shouldn't fight unless it can survive to evolution, which would need to be imminent in order for it to live that long with its low HP
Fury Attack primary, Supersonic probably shouldn't get used
Wall-ness boost from Smokescreen
Tail Wrap primary

Rapids is a 50/50 chance at Energy Denial, and Energy Denial is disproportionately valuable (though still dampened by the coin flip). However, Water Punch calls for Over-Attach with an unlimited cap, but this card's evolution only takes 4 energies max. Therefore, this card should probably be capped at 4 since the benefit of more isn't very good. I don't know which move should be primary. Let the bot sort it out
Same Call For Friend logic as other cards
No logic needed, mark green
Clamp primary, probably safe to mark green
Swift does 20 damage no matter what and can't be blocked, and should be priced a such

Jellyfish Pod is the primary unless the bot's hand already has 2 or more tentacool evolutions. Priced slightly differently to other moves that summon their own evolution, as it only summons it until its owner's hand rather than as an immediate evolution. Therefore, it's more suceptible to death on the opponent's next turn
Main attack is energy denial, which is valuable. It should possibly even get a wall-ness boost if able to deny the energy needed for an attack. That's another extra mile item
